# A page title, not decoration, and it does two jobs.
#
# 1. The metadata surfaces. Quarto composes `<title>`, `og:title` and
#    `twitter:title` from this plus the site title. With `title: ""` the two
#    social surfaces rendered as "– Robbins Analytics" — a dangling separator on
#    every shared card and every scrape of the landing page — while `<title>`
#    fell back to the bare site title. Every other page on the site carries a
#    title and rendered correctly; only the landing page did not.
#
# 2. The hero's own H1. With no title metadata, Quarto promotes the document's
#    first level-1 heading to be the title — so `# Aaron Robbins` was lifted OUT
#    of .hero-lede into the title block above the dark banner, and the hero
#    rendered starting at the subtitle with no name in it. `.hero-banner h1` in
#    styles.scss (white, 2.5rem, serif) had therefore never applied to anything.
#    Setting a title here leaves the heading where it was written.
#
# `body-classes` is the third piece: with a title set, Quarto renders its own
# title block above the hero, which would restate the name twice. styles.scss
# hides it on this class. `title-block-style: none` is NOT the way to do that —
# it still emits the heading AND emits a second <header id="title-block-header">,
# which is a duplicate id and an axe failure.
title: "Aaron Robbins, Senior / Staff / Principal Analyst"
body-classes: hero-page
image: https://www.robbinsanalytics.com/assets/thumb-portfolio.png
page-layout: full
toc: false
image-alt: "Cascadia module card — title, one-line summary, and the data source."

### Cascadia Revenue Assurance
<span class="badge-status new">New</span><span class="badge-status">Published</span>

What a customer is contracted for and what they are billable for are different numbers. Three asymmetric timing rules — adds land at once, reductions wait for the term boundary, cancellations ride out the term — keep the two apart for up to a year, with nothing erroring and no register showing it: 5,875 licences at June 2026. Derived twice, by two engines written to be different, agreeing on every cell. Synthetic data throughout.

[View Case Study](projects/cascadia-revenue-assurance.qmd){.btn .btn-primary .btn-sm}

### Cascadia Fee Examiner
<span class="badge-status new">New</span><span class="badge-status">Published</span>

A bankruptcy research database, a public court docket, and two task-code vocabularies — three sources, three owners, none sharing an identifier. A stated rule resolves 9 of 25 caption-to-database firm pairs; the other 16 are published with a reason, not dropped. Reported at its actual state: 48 of 216 eligible cases searched so far.

### Cascadia Matter Ledger
<span class="badge-status">Published</span>

Eleven million public federal civil case records, frozen and hash-verified, modelled into certified legal-operations measures — then a scheduled pipeline that re-asserts its own invariants twice a day, reconciles against the frozen baseline, and publishes the failures. Ask it one ordinary question and the ungoverned answer comes back negative.

[View Case Study](projects/cascadia-matter-ledger.qmd){.btn .btn-primary .btn-sm}

### Cascadia Control Tower
<span class="badge-status">Published</span>

Three fill rates computed from one dataset, all arithmetically correct and 7.0 points apart — and a split-shipment cost that none of them measures. Certifies one definition, prices the leak against a modelled no-split counterfactual, and shows why no single split threshold works across two banners. Synthetic operations, anchored to BLS, Census and SEC data.

[View Case Study](projects/cascadia-controltower.qmd){.btn .btn-primary .btn-sm}
[Fill Rate & Split Cost](https://www.robbinsanalytics.com/cascadia-controltower/){.btn .btn-outline-secondary .btn-sm}
:::

### The Combinatorics of Sibling Conflict
<span class="badge-status">Preprint</span>

Not an analytics module — a short mathematics paper. The number of ways n children can take sides against each other, with the rest uninvolved, is (3^n^ − 2·2^n^ + 1)/2, the Stirling number S(n+1, 3). Of the 25 ways four children can, 6 are one against one; of the 3,025 ways eight children can, 28 are.

[Read It](projects/sibling-conflict.qmd){.btn .btn-primary .btn-sm}
[The Paper (PDF)](https://www.robbinsanalytics.com/assets/Robbins-Combinatorics-of-Sibling-Conflict.pdf){.btn .btn-outline-secondary .btn-sm}
